# Draft:Venezuelan Trade During the Age of Revolutions

Trade Between Venezuela and the United States During the Age of Revolution
Introduction
Venezuela during the Age of Revolution refers to the opening of trade between the United States and Venezuela during the late 18th century and early 20th century. It refers to the commercial exchange of goods in Venezuelan ports especially within La Guaira and Puerto Cabello. This trade would emerge from the breakdown of Spanish mercantilism and regulations due to European wars such as the French Revolution and the Napoleonic Wars (Pompien, 2022, pp. 19-21). Due to strategic value of the United States and its proximity to Venezuela, mercantilists policies were abolished as to prevent Venezuela from collapsing due to Spanish absence. (p. 24)
Venezuelan authorities and elites would use neutral trade from the U.S to prevent famine, shortages, and raise revenue within the colony. Further one, revolutionary leaders such as Simon Bolivar would use this neutral trade to supply and finance the revolutionary effort. Although some saw American trade as enforcing colonial rule, others would use it to begin efforts of independence. Commercial conflict, monopolistic practices, and the state owned “Almacen del Rey would create resentment and contributed significant demand for autonomy and eventually independence. This would culminate in the First Venezuelan Republic as neutral and free trade would be one of its main rallying points (pp, 159-161).
Spanish Mercantilism and its Collapse
Before the late eighteenth century, Venezuela was controlled by a strict mercantilist system under Spanish rule. The colony would have no control over who it could trade to but would exclusively trade with Spain and only Spanish ships. Foreign trade was prohibited under this strict system of commerce and many of the goods and products produced within Venezuela would be exported and sold to Spain. However, trade was beneficially to Spanish Iberia rather than the colony itself. The French Revolution and the Napoleonic Wars weakened Spain significantly. This would affect the nations’ ability and efforts to enforce its policy of mercantilism on Venezuela. Moreover, general European conflict disrupted shipping and trade to Venezuela.
During these turbulent times, Venezuela would face many challenges. Shortages of goods, famine, and no way of financing itself, Venezuela saw itself in a precarious position. With little help from Spain, colonial officials and elites would accept the policy of “Comercio neutral” (neutral commerce/trade) in 1797. Venezuelan authorities would overlook and encourage free trade to help its position and adapt during Spanish absence. Particularly from the United States, trade was seen as a positive benefit as it would provide local needs. “Prosperity,” “happiness,” and “conservation” were treated as incredibly urgent over the adherence of mercantilism (p. 41). Venezuela before the opening of free trade was describe as a “unprovided province” (p. 25) with the amount of produce rotting without constant shipping.
Emergence of the United States and Trade
The United States would capitalize on trade and would flourish. Accounts describe that in La Guaira in 1798 that it was “impossible to miss the U.S flag” (pg. 23) when it came to merchant vessels offshore and within the ports itself. Trade would increase in the late 1790s as voyages between Venezuela and the United States would increase from 19 in 1797 to more than 122 in 1799 (p. 41). The United States would supply Venezuela with goods and materials such as wheat and grain staples, flour, manufactured foods, tools, and military supplies. Flour was seen as of particular importance as a hedge for urgent emergencies such as invasion, rebellion, or revolution (p. 73). Venezuela would also trade with the United States as well. Tropical produce such as cocoa and tobacco was exported (p. 42)
There were two types of trade: private and contracting trade. The former would be market driven between Venezuelan merchants and planters and U.S traders. This would connect average Venezuelans to the broader Atlantic markets. The latter would be considered Spanish government trade. United States merchants would function as contractors for the colonial state. Many valuable goods such as tobacco would be shipped abroad in bulk in exchange for necessary goods such as flour or slaves. These merchants would also receive exemption from duties and would obtain Spanish consular documentation such as with Royal Tobacco to traverse and move goods through transatlantic routes (pp. 57-58). This trade was more valuable, and this was tied to imperial needs. This would strengthen colonial finances and the military Particularly in the military, imports would be used for barracks, hospitals, garrisons, and to supply other strategic provinces (p. 73).
Almacen del Rey and Monopolistic Conflict
Trade between the United States and Venezuela was lucrative and would be seen as necessary to keep Venezuela from imploding. Due to the excess of materials and goods such as flour and textiles, the colonial government would create a market where regular commoners could purchase these goods directly from the government, this was called the “Almacen del Rey” (The King’s Store). This store, however, would inflate prices of these goods significantly and were seen as wartime prices (pp. 86-88). Many people saw this trade as a monopoly as only through the government could anyone purchase these goods. It would be seen as “tyranny” (pg. 145) and an attempt to extract as much revenue as possible from commoners. This would create unrest between colonial officials, Venezuelan elites, and local merchants, which added to discontent with colonial rule.
Trade during the First Venezuelan Republic
During 1809-1810, Venezuelan officials feared of increasing dependency on United States. Due to circumstances in Spain and with increasing fear of U.S port closures and war erupting with Britain, Venezuela sought to “stock itself with flour from the United States.” (pg. 165) On April 19, 1810, the Junta Suprema Conservada de los Derechos de Fernando VII would form in Caracas. This was an autonomous governing body that would expel colonial officials and push Venezuela further from Spanish control to political independence. On July 5, 1811, the First Venezuelan Republic formed (pp. 159-160).
Venezuelans though that freer trade would bring new sovereignty as well as forge friends and alliances but was impractical due to current administrative and financial infrastructure. Trade with the United States would bring the same goods such as food supplies and generate customs receipts. U.S merchants were crucial to Venezuelan independence which bought the sales of guns, gunpowder, and provisions to Venezuela (p. 161). However, due to neutrality, there were a few U.S merchants who chose to supply imperial Spain which hindered the First Venezuelan Republics effort for independence. Moreover, free trade alone could not sustain the current political climate of Venezuela which faced internal affairs, monetary weakness, and military challenges.
Disruption of Trade and the Collapse of the First Republic
With the collapse of the Republic in 1812, the trade relationship did not stop. Prior to the republics collapse, American shipping declined in Venezuela due to wider wartime effects in the United States and U.S embargoes for Venezuelan elites would be a factor within the collapse of the republic. The trade relationship, however, transformed in two ways. One was with imperial Spain, who had control of most ports within Venezuela and where most U.S merchants would trade with as it was safe and legally encouraged. 4/5ths of American trade went into Spanish royalist-controlled ports where regulation was familiar, and risks were low (pp. 192-193)
In comparison, some U.S traders would conduct business with rebels and revolutionary leaders. This trade was seen as more challenging as it was seen as illegal but also due to constant strains of port control. Furthermore, rebel groups often had little monetary compensation to these traders and thus, merchants were faced with higher insurance costs, delayed payments, unreliable credit, and the perception that revolutionary efforts would end up in failure. Commerce was still seen as important for revolutionary efforts, but with the growing number of traders in Spanish controlled ports, some described it as “business arithmetic.” (pg. 245)
Business Arithmetic
U.S neutrality allowed merchants to trade with royalist Spain, but moreover this was seen as a betrayal from revolutionary leaders and would be a central grievance point in post-Venezuelan independence. American merchants would supply both Spanish royalists and rebels during the revolution. Some believed that these merchants procured profit rather than by principle. American traders supplied arms, provisions, and shipping services to whoever controlled ports whether Spanish or Venezuelan rebels.
Following Venezuelan independence, Venezuela trade would heavily rely on foreign merchants due to its precarious position post-independence. Supplies, shipping, and credits became essential for Venezuela to survive. Due to this, American traders and European traders would exploit this vulnerable situation by providing overpriced contracts, speculative pricing, and corrupt arrangements especially within the military. This would only exacerbate the fiscal crisis and reinforce perceptions of commerce abroad. (p. 247-248). While originally trade was seen to provide Venezuela a new way of independence, in some instances, U.S trade would hinder by exploiting trade in a state that was in turmoil.
